Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I dwell on how the event could have been prevented
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
I try to erase the memory of the event

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
The world is a dangerous place
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Sexual Objectification: Being looked at sexually
issues.explanation: For a 78-year-old woman whose index trauma is a natural disaster, this trigger is clinically hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other triggers, appraisals, memory items, and strategies all fit disaster-related loss/danger themes, but 'being looked at sexually' implies a sexual-threat/sexual-trauma context that is not represented anywhere else in the formulation or item set. This is more than unusual; it introduces a qualitatively different trauma meaning network without supporting items in Threat, Memory, Appraisals, or Strategies.

vignette: Martha, a 78-year-old European-American graphic designer, has been struggling with the aftermath of a natural disaster that occurred several months ago. The event left her feeling profoundly shaken and changed her perspective on life in ways she never imagined possible. The traumatic experience began with a sudden storm that devastated her community. Martha vividly recalls the sound of doors opening and slamming as the wind wreaked havoc, breaking windows and causing chaos inside her home. Since then, any noise resembling that of a door can trigger intense feelings of fear and unease. Talking about people losing loved ones also deeply disturbs her, as she narrowly escaped losing her husband during the disaster. The lingering smell of alcohol in public places brings back memories of the chaos and destruction, further exacerbating her distress. Martha has come to believe that the world is a dangerous place where injustice prevails, and what happened to her was deeply unfair. This shattered her beliefs about how the world works and left her feeling vulnerable and insecure. These negative appraisals have led her to engage in maladaptive strategies such as ruminating on how the event could have been prevented and compulsively cleaning or organizing things repeatedly to regain a sense of control. Martha frequently finds herself dwelling on these thoughts, especially at work where she is surrounded by others who might discuss the disaster. The sound of doors opening during meetings can be particularly distressing, leading her to feel like the memory is happening right now rather than something that has passed. This feeling of being present in the moment makes it difficult for her to focus on her design projects and often leads her to leave early or avoid work altogether. She also tries to erase the memory of the event entirely, but this only amplifies the emotional numbness she experiences when recalling what happened. Martha feels as if the extreme nature of the disaster is so unreal that it's hard to believe it actually occurred to her. These intense emotions and thoughts are reinforced by her persistent fear of triggers, which in turn fuel her negative appraisals about the world. Over time, this cycle has worsened Martha’s condition. Her husband has noticed a significant change in her behavior—she is more withdrawn and frequently expresses feelings of despair. The compulsion to clean and organize intensifies during periods when she feels particularly overwhelmed by memories and triggers. She cleans her home compulsively to feel a semblance of control, yet this only provides temporary relief before the cycle begins anew. Martha’s work as a graphic designer has suffered significantly; she often misses deadlines and finds it difficult to collaborate with colleagues. The pressure at work makes her rumination worse, leading her to avoid social gatherings or any situation where doors might open suddenly. This avoidance has strained her relationships with friends and coworkers, leaving her feeling increasingly isolated. What finally brought Martha to seek help was the realization that she could no longer cope on her own. She is most afraid of losing control completely and being unable to function in her daily life. Despite this fear, she is hopeful that therapy can provide some relief from these overwhelming feelings and help her regain a sense of normalcy. Martha’s story underscores how the traumatic event has not only affected her immediate reactions but also deeply ingrained negative beliefs about herself and the world around her. The cycle of triggers, maladaptive strategies, and distorted memories continues to reinforce her negative appraisals, leaving her feeling stuck and unable to move forward without intervention.
